short_alt_draft: Stacked bar charts of CES-vetted LLM success rates across bug prediction, localization, and repair tasks.
long_description_draft: This figure contains three side-by-side groups of stacked bar charts, one each for bug prediction, bug localization, and bug repair, with ten LLMs (CodeLlama-Inst-34b, MagiCoder-S-6.7b, DeepSeekCoder-Inst-33b, SemCoder-S-6.7b, StarCoder-15b, Gemini-1.5-Pro, GPT4, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and o4-mini) shown per group. Each bar spans 0–100% and is divided into four colored segments representing categories from the Correctness Evaluation Survey (CES): confident success (green, bottom), suspicious success (blue-gray), likely success (orange), and incoherent (yellow, top). Across all three tasks, the orange "likely success" and yellow "incoherent" segments generally make up large portions of most bars, while green "confident success" segments are comparatively small, indicating that a sizable share of outputs judged successful by standard metrics are actually flagged as unreliable or incoherent under closer human/automated vetting. The relative size of each colored segment varies by model and task, but exact percentage values for individual bars are not legible from the image.
critiques: [Ashub Shafqat, verdict=Yes] The LLM-generated short alt text and long description accurately capture the three task panels, all ten LLM labels, the four CES color categories, and the overall trend while noting that exact bar percentages are not legible; however, the Figure type override dropdown was pre-set to "other" instead of "chart" and had to be corrected.

short_alt_draft: Stacked bar chart showing prefill vs decoding phase share of LLM inference latency across log datasets.
long_description_draft: This is a stacked bar chart with a y-axis labeled "Latency Attribution" ranging from 0% to 100%, and an x-axis labeled "ith Log Dataset" showing roughly 15 individual bars, each representing a different log dataset (specific dataset names are not legible). Each bar is divided into two segments: a pink lower segment labeled "Prefill Phase" and a gray upper segment labeled "Decoding Phase." Across nearly all bars, the prefill phase segment dominates, occupying roughly 75-90% of total latency, while the decoding phase makes up the remaining smaller portion. The chart visually supports the paper's finding that prefill latency, not decoding, is the primary bottleneck in LLM inference for online log parsing, averaging about 85% of total latency across datasets.
critiques: [Ashub Shafqat, verdict=Yes] The LLM-generated short alt text and long description accurately identify the chart type, axes, legend categories, and the dominant 75–90% share of the Prefill Phase across datasets, though the draft estimates roughly 15 bars instead of the exact 16 bars shown and describes the omitted x-axis tick labels as "not legible."

short_alt_draft: Diagram comparing full KV recompute vs. prefix caching across three sequential requests with shared blocks.
long_description_draft: The figure has two side-by-side panels, each showing three requests (req1, req2, req3) arriving in time order, with each request's sequence of labeled blocks (b1 through b9) shown as adjacent colored boxes, ending in a decoding block. In panel (a), "Recompute," all blocks in every request are shown in the same yellow color and labeled "prefill," meaning every block, even ones matching earlier requests, is recomputed from scratch before the final decoding block. In panel (b), "Prefix caching," matching leading blocks shared with a prior request are highlighted in darker orange and labeled "Loading KV" (for example, req2 reuses b1,b2 from req1, and req3 reuses b1,b2,b3 from req1/req2), while remaining non-matching blocks are labeled "prefill" and are recomputed even if they appear in an earlier request, as seen with req3's b7,b8 which match req2's blocks in position but cannot be reused because the preceding block b6 differs. This contrast illustrates that prefix caching avoids recomputation only for an exact, order-dependent shared prefix, while any mismatch earlier in the sequence forces later matching blocks to be recomputed anyway.
critiques: [Ashub Shafqat, verdict=Yes] The LLM-generated short alt text and long description accurately explain the two-panel comparison between Recompute and Prefix caching, including the time progression across req1–req3, the color-coded phases (Loading KV, prefill, decoding), and why blocks b7 and b8 in req3 must be recomputed; however, the Figure type override dropdown was pre-set to "chart" instead of "diagram" and had to be corrected.

short_alt_draft: Three line charts comparing KD methods vs fine-tuning for RoBERTa students across three tasks and model sizes.
long_description_draft: This figure contains three stacked line charts, each showing performance of RoBERTa student models at three sizes (30M, 7M, and 1.5M parameters) on the x-axis, from larger to smaller. The top chart shows Accuracy for Defect Detection, the middle shows F1 score for Clone Detection, and the bottom shows Top-1 Accuracy for Exception Classification. Each chart plots five lines representing standard fine-tuning (FT) and four knowledge distillation methods (KD, DIST, PKD, CKD), plus a dashed horizontal reference line labeled "Teacher" showing the UniXcoder teacher model's performance. In all three charts, performance generally declines as model size decreases, with FT consistently the lowest-performing line and the distillation methods (especially CKD, and DIST for exception classification) staying closer to the teacher's performance, illustrating that knowledge distillation helps smaller student models retain more of the teacher's accuracy than plain fine-tuning.
critiques: [Areej rashid, verdict=No] The original description offers greater detail on the knowledge distillation method, incorporating numerical values from the graphs to support observations across different RoBERTa models. In contrast, the LLM-generated description is overly generic. It merely states what each graph plots without comparing the performance of the methods against one another or across the evaluated models.

short_alt_draft: Flowchart of 8-step pipeline: hazard analysis through test execution to fault tree visualization.
long_description_draft: This flowchart illustrates a two-phase process for testing small uninhabited aerial systems (sUAS), with steps numbered 1 through 8 connected by arrows. In Phase 1 (top row), a domain expert or sUAS developer performs hazard analysis (step 1), which feeds into defining fuzz specifications and test mission specifications (steps 2-3), used to create a decision-tree test oracle (step 4). In Phase 2 (bottom row), this oracle informs a test configuration generator/fuzzer, which works with an execution handler (covering simulation environment, system under test, and field testing) and execution storage to run test cases (step 5). Results flow into a mission execution profile, which undergoes decision tree analysis and failure identification via result clustering (step 6), generating minimal fault trees (step 7) that are visualized (step 7) and used to loop back into failure/root cause analysis feeding back to the domain expert (step 8). Overall, the diagram shows an automated pipeline linking hazard analysis, fuzz testing, and fault tree generation for sUAS safety testing.
critiques: [Abdul Razzaq, verdict=Yes] The diagram shows a flow from a structured JSON defect pattern specification at the top down, to a concrete Python code snippet at the bottom. short_alt_draft: Flowchart of RefAgent's multi-agent refactoring pipeline with context tools, generation, compile and test loops.
long_description_draft: This diagram shows the architecture of RefAgent, a multi-agent system for automated code refactoring, as a flowchart with numbered steps 1 through 6. A Java file feeds into a Context Retrieval Tool and Code Search Module, which extract dependent classes, quality metrics, and source code (labeled A, B, C); these feed a Context-aware Planner Agent that builds a Context-aware Prompt and generates a refactoring plan. This plan and context (B, C) pass to the Refactoring Generator Agent, which produces a refactored class and sends it to the Compiler Agent (using a Maven compiler tool), looping up to 20 times on failure before returning error or success. On compiler success, the Tester Agent runs EvoSuite and Maven test tools, also looping up to 20 times on failure; if all tests pass the refactored code is kept, otherwise after 20 failed iterations the original code is retained. The diagram visually emphasizes that the Refactoring Generator Agent is called repeatedly by the Compiler and Tester Agents to fix errors while still following the original refactoring plan.
critiques: [Faseeh Ansari, verdict=Yes] The description is accurate. The only thing is the figure type: it should be “diagram”, not “other”.
[ALI ASLAM, verdict=Yes] The second paragraph explains the RefAgent architecture and how the agents work together.

short_alt_draft: Code diff for Issue #9590: Wasm bytecode (left) and x86-64 Wasmtime output (right).
long_description_draft: This figure shows two numbered code listings side by side, formatted as a diff with removed lines highlighted in red/pink and added lines highlighted in green. The left panel (lines 1-20) contains WebAssembly bytecode for a function with nested loops and an if block, where a "local.get" instruction (removed) is replaced by an equivalent "f64.const" instruction (added) near the end. The right panel (lines 21-44) shows the corresponding x86-64 assembly code generated by Wasmtime, containing labeled sections (START1, START2, BRANCH_TRUE, BRANCH_FALSE, END1, END2) with conditional branches; several lines are removed, including register spill/reload instructions using "movdqu" with the stack pointer (%rsp) and additional jump/branch instructions, while simpler "jne" branch instructions are added in their place. The overall takeaway, per the paper's discussion, is that the original (unmutated) program's compiled code contains extra register spills, reloads, and branches inside a loop compared to the mutated version, and these extra instructions are the direct cause of the performance slowdown identified for Issue #9590. Some fine details of the assembly operands, such as specific register names, may be hard to read at small sizes.

short_alt_draft: Diagram comparing three methods to remove sensitive data memorized by code language models.
long_description_draft: This diagram shows a model provider training a code language model (CLM) on a dataset containing sensitive information, such as a masked user_config code snippet with username, password, and email fields, and deploying the CLM; a user then sends a deletion request invoking the "Right To Be Forgotten." Three mitigation approaches branch from the training dataset and deployed model: (a) Data De-duplication, where duplicate data is removed and the CLM is fully retrained, taking about 900 A100 GPU days; (b) Differential Privacy, where retraining uses a formal privacy guarantee equation (Pr[A(D)] ≤ e^ε·Pr[A(D')] + δ) and produces a "locked" retrained CLM, taking about 1800 A100 GPU days; and (c) Machine Unlearning, where gradient ascent is applied directly to the deployed model to produce an "unlearned" CLM, taking only about 0.001 A100 GPU days. Each method is depicted with its own neural-network icon (pink, blue, and green nodes respectively) to visually distinguish the resulting model. The figure's key takeaway is the dramatic difference in computational cost among the three approaches, with unlearning being vastly faster, though the text notes it still struggles to selectively erase small sensitive segments without harming surrounding code.

short_alt_draft: Diagram of CREME: perturb prompt, localize key LLM layer, then edit it for robustness.
long_description_draft: This diagram shows the three-stage CREME framework as a left-to-right flow. On the left, an original code prompt and a perturbed version (with inserted typos, deletions, swaps, etc.) are shown as example inputs. In the middle "Key Layer Localization" panel, two stacked transformer diagrams (each with rows of hidden-state circles, attention boxes, and MLP diamonds) represent the unrobust LLM processing the original versus perturbed prompt; a highlighted layer's hidden states are swapped between the two runs, and the resulting code outputs are compared via a "Pass Rate" and "Recovery" score to identify the single most robustness-sensitive "key layer." On the right, the "Layer Editing" panel shows this key layer being fine-tuned using two loss terms, Loss1 (preservation loss, keeping behavior correct on clean inputs) and Loss2 (alignment loss, matching representations between original and perturbed prompts), producing an "Edited LLM." Overall, the figure illustrates how CREME pinpoints and then modifies one internal layer of a code LLM to make it more robust to small prompt perturbations.

short_alt_draft: Diagram of Type-aware Logic Matching (T4) comparing two transaction traces by token type.
long_description_draft: This diagram illustrates the T4 "Type-aware Logic Similarity Matching" process from a DeFi attack detection pipeline. At the top, a gray box shows a stored pattern trace labeled "<The Word Project>" listing a sequence of operations like flashloan, transfer, approve, and swapExactTokens. Below, two green boxes (Layer 1 and Layer 2) show the extracted logic for Transaction A and Transaction B after the T3 extraction step, with operations color-coded blue for core asset tokens and black for protocol-specific tokens. A third gray box shows a similarly structured "Target Trace" with a hexadecimal contract address. At the bottom, a red box computes the Asymmetrical Normalized Set Difference (ANSD) separately for core asset and protocol-specific token sets, showing example set sizes and differences both equal to zero, feeding into a weighted final similarity score (Sim = λ·core + (1−λ)·proto = 1). The overall takeaway is that by separating operations by token type and comparing them with a noise-robust set-difference metric, the method reliably matches attack traces despite reordering or extra noise operations.
